s0101.literal: In the first year of Tianjia he was summoned as Attendant-in-Ordinary and Minister of the Masters of Writing for Capital Offenses, but before taking office he was again made Director of the Secretariat.
s0101.idiomatic: In Tianjia year one he was called up as attendant-in-ordinary and minister of capital offenses, but before he took up the post he was again made director of the secretariat.

s0102.literal: He was transferred to Tutor to the Crown Prince, acting administrator of the Eastern Palace, his post as Attendant-in-Ordinary unchanged.
s0102.idiomatic: He was made tutor to the crown prince and acting head of the eastern palace, keeping his attendant-in-ordinary rank.

s0103.literal: He was given the rank of Grandee with the Golden Horse and Grand Seal and concurrently held the post of Director of Revenue.
s0103.idiomatic: He was promoted to grandee with the golden horse seal and also directed the revenue office.

s0104.literal: When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, he was given the additional title of Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant.
s0104.idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor came to the throne he was made scattered-cavalry regular attendant as well.

s0105.literal: In the first year of Taijian he was transferred to Vice Director of the Masters of Writing (right).
s0105.idiomatic: In Taijian year one he was made right vice director of the masters of writing.

s0106.literal: At that time the eastern regions suffered great floods and the people were in famine; Mo was made General of Benevolent Martial Might and Administrator of Jinling.
s0106.idiomatic: The east was then stricken by flood and famine, and Mo was sent out as benevolent-martial general and administrator of Jinling.

s0107.literal: In the commandery he had great authority and kindness; the people of the commandery memorialized requesting a stele to praise Mo's achievements, and an edict approved it.
s0107.idiomatic: He governed Jinling with real authority and kindness; the people petitioned for a stele to his record and the court agreed.

s0108.literal: He was summoned as Supervisor of the Secretariat, again appointed Vice Director of the Masters of Writing (right), and concurrently Right Army General.
s0108.idiomatic: He was recalled as supervisor of the secretariat, again made right vice director of the masters of writing, and given the right army generalship.

s0109.literal: In the fifth month of the fourth year he died, aged sixty-seven.
s0109.idiomatic: He died in the fifth month of year four, at sixty-seven.

s0110.literal: He was posthumously made Attendant-in-Ordinary and Supervisor of the Secretariat, with the posthumous name Wen.
s0110.idiomatic: Posthumously he was made attendant-in-ordinary and supervisor of the secretariat, with the posthumous name Wen.

s0111.literal: Yuan Jing, courtesy name Zigong, was a man of Yangxia in Chen commandery.
s0111.idiomatic: Yuan Jing, styled Zigong, was from Yangxia in Chen commandery.

s0112.literal: His grandfather Yan was a Song Attendant-in-Ordinary, Minister of Personnel, and Inspector of Yongzhou.
s0112.idiomatic: His grandfather Yan had been a Song attendant-in-ordinary, minister of personnel, and inspector of Yongzhou.

s0113.literal: His father Ang was a Liang Attendant-in-Ordinary and Minister of Works, with the posthumous title Duke Mu.
s0113.idiomatic: His father Ang had been a Liang attendant-in-ordinary and minister of works, posthumously Duke Mu.

s0114.literal: Shu, courtesy name Jianyan, was the son of Junzheng, Administrator of Wu commandery under Liang.
s0114.idiomatic: Shu, styled Jianyan, was the son of Junzheng, Liang's administrator of Wu commandery.

s0115.literal: He had fine looks and a calm disposition, loved reading, and never put down his books.
s0115.idiomatic: He was handsome and reserved, loved books, and always had one in hand.

s0116.literal: His family for generations had been illustrious and wealthy, yet Shu alone lived plainly; he had no companions at his side, sat upright in a single room, and unless on public business never went abroad—his heart toward glory and profit was utterly indifferent.
s0116.idiomatic: Though his house was great and rich, Shu lived simply alone, kept no company, and sat in one room; he went out only on duty and cared nothing for rank or gain.

s0117.literal: He first entered office as a Liang Secretariat Gentleman, then served as Aide to the Crown Prince, Registrar to the Prince of Hedong of the Light Chariots, and Merit Clerk in the two prefectures of the preceding Prince of Shaoling and the Central Army Prince Xuan
s0117.idiomatic: He began as a Liang secretariat gentleman, then served as crown prince aide, registrar to the prince of Hedong of the light chariots, and merit clerk in the households of the former prince of Shaoling and the central army prince Xuan

s0120.literal: [6] During Hou Jing's rebellion Shu went to Wu commandery to visit his father and thereupon entered mourning for his father.
s0120.idiomatic: [6] In Hou Jing's rebellion Shu went to Wu commandery to see his father and then mourned his father's death.

s0121.literal: At the time the four quarters were in turmoil and men sought only to escape harm; Shu's conduct in mourning became known for supreme filial piety.
s0121.idiomatic: The realm was in chaos and men sought only to save themselves, but Shu's mourning won fame for deep filial piety.

s0122.literal: When Wang Sengbian pacified Hou Jing and held the capital, the gentry all rushed to call on him; Shu alone shut his doors and lived quietly, seeking no fame.
s0122.idiomatic: When Wang Sengbian took the capital after defeating Hou Jing, the elite flocked to him; Shu stayed indoors and sought no advancement.

s0123.literal: In the first year of Shaotai he was summoned as Supernumerary Attendant of the Yellow Gate.
s0123.idiomatic: In Shaotai year one he was summoned as supernumerary attendant of the yellow gate.

s0124.literal: Before he took office he was appointed Outer Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, concurrently Attendant-in-Ordinary.
s0124.idiomatic: Before he took up the post he was made outer scattered-cavalry regular attendant and attendant-in-ordinary at the same time.

s0125.literal: In the second year he concurrently held the post of Minister of Personnel.
s0125.idiomatic: In year two he also served as minister of personnel.

s0126.literal: That year he went out as Administrator of Wu commandery.
s0126.idiomatic: That year he was posted as administrator of Wu commandery.

s0127.literal: In the second year of Yongding he was summoned as Left Minister for the People.
s0127.idiomatic: In Yongding year two he was summoned as left minister for the people.

s0128.literal: Before he arrived he was changed to Attendant-in-Ordinary and put in charge of the great selections.
s0128.idiomatic: Before he took up that post he was made attendant-in-ordinary and put in charge of high appointments.

s0129.literal: In the third year he was transferred to Minister of the Masters of Writing for Capital Offenses, with charge of selections as before.
s0129.idiomatic: In year three he was made minister of capital offenses, still overseeing appointments.

s0130.literal: Shu was broadly learned with a strong memory and clearly understood old regulations.
s0130.idiomatic: Shu was widely read, had a strong memory, and knew the old rules well.

s0131.literal: Earlier, the Founder's eldest daughter, Princess Yongshi, had first been married to Qian Yi, Administrator of Chenliu, and bore a son Jie; [7] the princess and Jie had both died in the Liang era.
s0131.idiomatic: Earlier the Founder's eldest daughter, Princess Yongshi, had married Qian Yi, administrator of Chenliu, and borne a son Jie; [7] both princess and son had died under Liang.

s0132.literal: When the Founder received the Mandate, only the princess was posthumously enfeoffed.
s0132.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne, only the princess received a posthumous enfeoffment.

s0133.literal: At this time she was about to be buried; the Host-Guests Office of the Masters of Writing requested detailed deliberation, wishing to add Yi as Commandant of the Consort's Carriage and also to bestow an office on Jie.
s0133.idiomatic: As burial approached, the host-guests office of the masters of writing asked for a full ruling, proposing to make Yi commandant of the consort's carriage and to grant Jie an office as well.

s0134.literal: Shu argued: "In antiquity when a king's daughter married down, she was always given to a feudal lord; that the chief wife be of the same surname [8] is heard in the Gongyang tradition, and that chariots and dress not be tied to rank is plain in the poets' odes.
s0134.idiomatic: Shu argued: "Anciently a king's daughter married down only to feudal lords; that the chief wife share the surname [8] is in the Gongyang school, and that carriage and dress not be bound to rank appears in the Odes.

s0135.literal: When the Han house first rose, marquises married imperial daughters; from then on princesses were married down to plain clans.
s0135.idiomatic: At Han's rise marquises married imperial daughters; afterward princesses wed common families.

s0136.literal: The post of Commandant of the Consort's Carriage was established by Emperor Wu of Han; [9] sometimes it was lent to meritorious ministers, sometimes added for kin—hence in Wei, Cao Zhi petitioned to make the consort commandant and the carriage attendant a single title.
s0136.idiomatic: The consort commandant was created by Han Wudi; [9] it was sometimes given to meritorious ministers and sometimes to kin—hence Cao Zhi in Wei asked to merge consort commandant and carriage attendant into one title.

s0137.literal: The Qi Regulations of Offices say that whoever marries a princess must receive the title Commandant of the Consort's Carriage; from Wei and Jin onward this became the standard.
s0137.idiomatic: The Qi office regulations say that a princess's husband must be made consort commandant; from Wei and Jin on that was the rule.

s0138.literal: This was because the king's daughter is weighty and a common surname is light: if her husband's rank were not raised, how could they share the cup and drink together? Hence the borrowed post of consort commandant was meant to honor the imperial daughter.
s0138.idiomatic: A king's daughter outranked a common house; without raising the husband's rank they could not share the marriage cup—so the consort commandant honored the princess.

s0139.literal: Now the princess died early and the marriage bond is severed; since no ritual question remains, why is the consort commandant needed?
s0139.idiomatic: The princess is long dead and the marriage ended; with no ritual issue left, why grant a consort commandant?

s0140.literal: Consider Du Yu, who married the second daughter of Jin's Emperor Xuan, Princess Gao Ling Xuan; when Jin's Emperor Wu took the throne the princess was already dead, and in the Taishi era she was posthumously enfeoffed as princess—Yu received no consort commandant title.
s0140.idiomatic: Du Yu married Jin Xuandi's second daughter, Princess Gao Ling Xuan; when Jin Wudi came to the throne she was already dead, and though she was enfeoffed posthumously in Taishi, Yu was never called consort commandant.

s0143.literal: [Wen] Emperor's daughter, Princess Xin'an Mu, died early; [10] at the beginning of Tianjian the Wang clan received no retrospective appointment.
s0143.idiomatic: [Wen] Emperor's daughter Princess Xin'an Mu died young; [10] at the start of Tianjian the Wangs were given no retrospective title.

s0144.literal: These two precedents, near and far, suffice as proof.
s0144.idiomatic: These two cases, ancient and recent, are proof enough.

s0145.literal: The princess's son had not yet reached the rites of adulthood, so this appointment is needless; now he should be posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Ting.
s0145.idiomatic: The princess's son had not reached adulthood and needs no such title; he should be enfeoffed posthumously as marquis of ting.

s0146.literal: " At the time Shu's argument was adopted.

s0147.literal: In the first year of Tianjia he acted as Minister of Personnel.
s0147.idiomatic: In Tianjia year one he acted as minister of personnel.

s0148.literal: In the third year he was confirmed in the post.
s0148.idiomatic: In year three he was confirmed in office.

s0149.literal: Soon he concurrently held the post of Right Army General and also served as Intendant of Danyang, his original posts unchanged.
s0149.idiomatic: He soon added right army general and intendant of Danyang, keeping his other posts.

s0150.literal: In the fifth year, because he was burying his father, he submitted a memorial resigning his posts; an edict granted fifty bolts of silk and a hundred thousand cash and ordered that after the burial he remain at home overseeing commandery affairs,
s0150.idiomatic: In year five, while burying his father, he asked to resign; the court gave fifty bolts of silk and a hundred thousand cash and told him to stay home after the funeral and still oversee commandery business,

s0152.literal: and when mourning ended [11] he returned to his original posts.
s0152.idiomatic: and when mourning ended [11] he resumed his former offices.

s0153.literal: That year his term ended; he was relieved of the intendant post and given Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant; his generalship and ministership remained as before.
s0153.idiomatic: When his term ended he left the intendant post, was made scattered-cavalry regular attendant, and kept his generalship and ministry.

s0154.literal: At that time the Vice Director Dao Zhongju, though he shared in selections, the weighing and promotion largely came from Shu; his recommendations mostly matched the sovereign's intent.
s0154.idiomatic: Though Vice Director Dao Zhongju shared appointments, Shu largely controlled selection and his nominees usually pleased the throne.

s0155.literal: Careful and thorough, he kept himself pure; civil and military officials rarely visited his door.
s0155.idiomatic: Careful, discreet, and upright, he had few visitors from office, civil or military.

s0156.literal: When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, he was transferred to Vice Director of the Masters of Writing (left).
s0156.idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor came to the throne he was made left vice director of the masters of writing.

s0157.literal: In the first year of Guangda he died, aged fifty-one.
s0157.idiomatic: He died in Guangda year one, at fifty-one.

s0158.literal: He was posthumously made Attendant-in-Ordinary and Left Grandee with the Glorious Credentials, with the posthumous name Jianyi.
s0158.idiomatic: Posthumously he was made attendant-in-ordinary and left grandee with glorious credentials, with the posthumous name Jianyi.

s0159.literal: A collection of ten juan circulated in his day.
s0159.idiomatic: A collection in ten juan circulated in his lifetime.

s0160.literal: His younger brother Xian has a separate biography.
s0160.idiomatic: His younger brother Xian has his own biography.

s0161.literal: The historian says: Wang Chong and Wang Tong, as scions of noble houses, early rose to pure office, yet faithfully observed ritual and served the throne with deep sincerity—this is admirable.
s0161.idiomatic: The historian writes: Wang Chong and Wang Tong, born to privilege and early raised to high office, still kept the rites and served faithfully—here is what deserves praise.

s0162.literal: Wang Mo's spirit was calm and detached; Yuan Shu's integrity was deep and hidden; though restraint and release differed in form, their excellence was of one measure—the famed gentlemen of old, were they not such men as these?
s0162.idiomatic: Wang Mo's mind was serene and Yuan Shu's conduct grave; one held back and one withdrew, yet both excelled alike—the "eminent men" of antiquity were surely such as these.

s0164.literal: Enfeoffed as Marquis of Andong ting because he was the emperor's nephew-by-marriage—"Andong" in the History of the Southern Dynasties reads "Dongan."
s0164.idiomatic: On "enfeoffed as marquis of Andong ting as the emperor's nephew": the Southern Dynasties history reads Dongan.

s0165.literal: Father Lin, Chief Clerk of the Director of the Masters of Works—"Director of the Masters of Works" in the Northern Supervisor, Ji, and Palace editions reads "Minister of Works."
s0165.idiomatic: On "father Lin, chief clerk of the director of the masters of works": Northern Supervisor, Ji, and Palace editions read minister of works.

s0166.literal: According to Qian Daxin's Examination of the Twenty-Two Histories, this is a different Wang Lin.
s0166.idiomatic: Qian Daxin's Examination of the Twenty-Two Histories notes that this is a different Wang Lin.

s0167.literal: Rapid Cavalry Prince of Luling's mansion Giver-in-Attendant—Zhang Senkai
s0167.idiomatic: Rapid Cavalry Prince of Luling's mansion giver-in-attendant—Zhang Senkai

s0169.literal: says: "'Giver' is suspect and should read 'follow'; the office regulations have no giver-in-attendant."
s0169.idiomatic: writes: "'Giver' is probably 'follow'; the office list has no giver-in-attendant."

s0170.literal: Mo, courtesy name Gongji—"Gongji" in the History of the Southern Dynasties and the Imperial Mirror 672 reads "Gongqi."
s0170.idiomatic: On "Mo styled Gongji": the Southern Dynasties history and Imperial Mirror 672 read Gongqi.

s0172.literal: [Mo] concurrently Chief Clerk of the Chancellor—changed according to the Northern Supervisor, Ji, and Palace editions.
s0172.idiomatic: On "[Mo] concurrently chief clerk of the chancellor": emended per Northern Supervisor, Ji, and Palace editions.

s0173.literal: Preceding Prince of Shaoling, Central Army Prince Xuan
s0173.idiomatic: Preceding prince of Shaoling, central army prince Xuan

s0175.literal: [City] Wang, merit clerk in two prefectures—Zhang Senkai
s0175.idiomatic: [City] Wang, two prefectures' merit clerk—Zhang Senkai

s0177.literal: says: "'Cheng' should read 'city'; Liang had no Prince Xuan Cheng.
s0177.idiomatic: writes: "'Cheng' should be 'city'; Liang had no Prince Xuan Cheng.

s0178.literal: " According to the Biography of the Lamented Crown Prince in the Book of Liang, the eldest son of Emperor Jianwen, Daqi, was enfeoffed as Prince of Xuancheng commandery.
s0178.idiomatic: The Book of Liang's biography of the lamented crown prince shows Jianwen's eldest son Daqi enfeoffed as prince of Xuancheng.

s0179.literal: Zhang's view is correct; the text is now changed accordingly.
s0179.idiomatic: Zhang is right; the text is emended accordingly.

s0180.literal: Bore a son Jie—"Jie" was originally corrupt as another character; the other editions are not corrupt; it is now corrected.
s0180.idiomatic: On "bore a son Jie": the character was corrupt in the base text; other editions read correctly—now fixed.

s0182.literal: Same surname as chief—"chief" was originally corrupt as "king"; now corrected according to the Northern Supervisor, Ji, and Palace editions.
s0182.idiomatic: On "same surname as chief": zhu was corrupt as wang—emended per Northern Supervisor, Ji, and Palace editions.

s0183.literal: According to the source, this phrase comes from the Gongyang, Duke Zhuang year one.
s0183.idiomatic: The line comes from the Gongyang commentary, Duke Zhuang year one.

s0184.literal: The post of Commandant of the Consort's Carriage was established by Emperor Wu of Han—the character "by" in the original was effaced; it is now supplied from the various editions.
s0184.idiomatic: On "consort commandant established by Han Wudi": the character you was faded in the base text and is restored from other editions.

s0187.literal: [Wen] Emperor's daughter, Princess Xin'an Mu, died early—changed according to the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0187.idiomatic: On "[Wen] Emperor's daughter Princess Xin'an Mu died early": emended per the Southern Dynasties history.

s0188.literal: According to the note, after Emperor Wu of Liang took the throne he posthumously honored his father as Emperor Wen.
s0188.idiomatic: After Liang Wudi's accession he honored his father posthumously as Emperor Wen.

s0189.literal: The biography of Wang Chong says his mother was Emperor Wu of Liang's sister, Princess Xin'an Mu—this agrees.
s0189.idiomatic: Wang Chong's biography says his mother was Liang Wudi's sister Princess Xin'an Mu, which matches.

s0192.literal: When mourning ended—deleted according to the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0192.idiomatic: On "when mourning ended": omitted per the Southern Dynasties history.
